query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi reduces the stacking-fault energy and alters short-range order, increasing partial dislocation activity and twinning in FeNiCrMn at moderate to high strain rates and lower temperatures, thus shifting the dynamic strain-hardening response relative to the Co-containing baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi with controlled similar grain sizes and minimal coarse precipitates.
generation.intervention: Conduct high-strain-rate mechanical tests over varied temperatures while performing in-situ diffraction (X-ray or neutron) to track real-time changes in dislocation structures, stacking-fault density, and short-range order.
generation.conditions: Temperatures spanning cryogenic (~77 K) to ~600 K, at strain rates from 10^-3 to ~10^3 s^-1, comparing Co-free FeNiCrMn to CoCrFeMnNi under identical loading protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Concurrent evolution of partial dislocation glide, twinning, and short-range ordering under high strain rates and varying temperatures, probed by diffraction and electron microscopy.
generation.mechanism: Lower stacking-fault energy and altered local chemical ordering in FeNiCrMn promote more frequent partial dislocation nucleation and enhanced twinning, shifting the rate-sensitivity and temperature dependence of plastic flow compared to CoCrFeMnNi.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Co-containing baseline, FeNiCrMn will exhibit higher twinning activity and stronger strain hardening at lower to intermediate temperatures and elevated strain rates; at higher temperatures, these differences may diminish as thermally activated processes overshadow short-range-order effects.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested under matching strain rates and temperatures, with the same initial grain size and processing history.
generation.boundary: Microstructures remain single-phase FCC; both alloys retain stable grain size under test conditions; local chemical fluctuations leading to short-range order are not suppressed by excessive diffusion at higher temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: Whether short-range order differences will be consistently detectable in real-time at elevated strain rates remains to be established empirically.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare in-situ diffraction measurements of FeNiCrMn and CoCrFeMnNi during high-strain-rate compression at several temperatures to track real-time stacking-fault densities, dislocation substructures, and twinning incidence.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the extent of partial dislocation activity, twinning, and short-range order evolution in Co-free FeNiCrMn mirrors the CoCrFeMnNi reference under the same test conditions, the proposed mechanism of altered stacking-fault energy and SRO controlling strain-rate and temperature response is refuted.

However, the mechanism of the special phenomenon for the high-entropy alloy deformed at high strain rates (beyond 1 × 103 s−1) is not clear yet. Serration characteristics are ubiquitous in many structural and functional materials such as high-entropy alloy (AlCoCr1.5Fe1.5NiTi0.5, Al0.3CoCrFeNi etc.). It would lead to the instability of mechanical properties. By studying the serration behavior, it may be possible to have an early warning signal for oncoming epileptic seizures and perhaps economic trends. In the present work, we used the split-Hopkinson pressure bar to investigate the dynamic mechanical behavior of NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy prepared by arc melting. The aims are: (1) To report the mechanical properties and microstructure under dynamic loadings, (2) to obtain the plastic model, and (3) to discuss the microstructural mechanism for the serration behavior when the alloy deforms at high strain rates.

AbstractIn this study, we manufactured a non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 high-entropy alloy (HEA) consisting of a single-phase face-centered-cubic structure. We applied in situ neutron diffraction coupled with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to investigate its tensile properties, microstructural evolution, lattice strains and texture development, and the stacking fault energy. The non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 HEA revealed a good combination of strength and ductility in mechanical properties compared to the equiatomic CoNiCrFe HEA, due to both stable solid solution and precipitation-strengthened effects. The non-equiatomic stoichiometry resulted in not only a lower electronegativity mismatch, indicating a more stable state of solid solution, but also a higher stacking fault energy (SFE, ~50 mJ/m2) due to the higher amount of Ni and the lower amount of Cr. This higher SFE led to a more active motion of dislocations relative to mechanical twinning, resulting in severe lattice distortion near the grain boundaries and dislocation entanglement near the twin boundaries. Chemical short-range order in disordered solid solutions often emerges with specific heat treatments. Unlike thermally activated ordering, mechanically derived short-range order (MSRO) in a multi-principal-element Fe40Mn40Cr10Co10 (at%) alloy originates from tensile deformation at 77 K, and its degree/extent can be tailored by adjusting the loading rates under quasistatic conditions. The mechanical response and multi-length-scale characterisation pointed to the minor contribution of MSRO formation to yield strength, mechanical twinning, and deformation-induced displacive transformation. Scanning and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and the anlaysis of electron diffraction patterns revealed the microstructural features responsible for MSRO and the dependence of the ordering degree/extent on the applied strain rates. Here, we show that underpinned by molecular dynamics, MSRO in the alloys with low stacking-fault energies forms when loaded at 77 K, and these systems that offer different perspectives on the process of strain-induced ordering transition are driven by crystalline lattice defects (dislocations and stacking faults). decision.trend: Early studies on CoCrFeMnNi-type alloys demonstrated unusually high ductility and strength from enhanced dislocation activity and twinning, especially under low-temperature or high-strain-rate conditions. Subsequent work revealed the importance of stacking-fault energy, magnetic interactions, and short-range ordering in modifying deformation mechanisms. More recent micromechanical models connected precipitation and grain-boundary behaviors to flow stress. However, the specific temperature and strain-rate sensitivities of Co-free FeNiCrMn alloys have not been isolated in prior studies, leaving the mechanistic origin of their distinct dynamic response unexplained.
decision.unsolved: While CoCrFeMnNi and its derivatives have been extensively characterized, the absence of cobalt in FeNiCrMn changes the alloy’s magnetic and stacking-fault landscapes in ways not yet fully understood. The interplay of partial dislocation glide, twinning, and local chemical interactions at elevated strain rates and varying temperatures has not been conclusively explained, and the role of short-range ordering remains unclear. A comprehensive theoretical framework tying these factors to the distinct dynamic responses of Co-free compositions is still missing.
decision.lever: Perform high-strain-rate deformational experiments across a range of temperatures, capturing real-time lattice response via in-situ diffraction (X-ray or neutron) to evaluate the evolution of dislocation core structures, stacking-fault density, and short-range order changes, using equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi as the baseline for direct comparison.
decision.why: By comparing in-situ structural and mechanical responses under identical loading conditions for both Co-free FeNiCrMn and the reference Co-containing alloy, the hypothesized role of altered stacking-fault energies and dynamic short-range order can be confirmed or refuted. This approach directly tests whether the removal of Co modifies the onset of partial dislocation and twinning processes—or changes their relative contributions—thereby shaping high-strain-rate and temperature-dependent mechanical behavior. If the in-situ measurements do not reveal significant differences in fault density or dislocation activity under comparable conditions, the hypothesis that removing Co alters the rate and temperature dependence via short-range order must be rejected.
